lesson.title: From Sea to Shining Sea: The War That Redrew the Map
lesson.summary: The 1846 to 1848 war with Mexico, sparked by the annexation of Texas and a border dispute, delivered the Mexican Cession to the United States while reopening the explosive question of whether slavery would expand into the new territory.
lesson.body:
The annexation of Texas in 1845 brought the long simmering conflict between American expansion and Mexican sovereignty to a head. Mexico had never accepted the Republic of Texas as legitimate and considered its absorption into the United States an act of aggression. Making matters worse, the two countries disagreed sharply about where the Texas border actually lay: the United States claimed the Rio Grande as the boundary, while Mexico insisted on the Nueces River, well over a hundred miles further north and east.

President James K. Polk, an ardent believer in Manifest Destiny, ordered General Zachary Taylor to move American troops into the disputed zone between the two rivers. In April 1846, Mexican cavalry clashed with a patrol of American soldiers north of the Rio Grande, killing or capturing most of them. Polk used the incident to declare that Mexico had "shed American blood upon the American soil," and Congress declared war on May 13, 1846, though a minority, including a freshman Whig congressman named Abraham Lincoln, later challenged Polk's account of exactly where the blood had been shed.

The war unfolded on multiple fronts. Taylor pushed south into Mexico, winning battles at Palo Alto, Resaca de la Palma, and Monterrey before a costly victory at Buena Vista in February 1847. Meanwhile American settlers in California, aided by explorer John C. Fremont and naval forces, staged the Bear Flag Revolt in June 1846 and helped bring California under American control with little organized Mexican resistance in the north. The decisive campaign, however, belonged to General Winfield Scott, who landed an army at Veracruz in March 1847 and fought his way inland, capturing Mexico City itself in September 1847, the first time a foreign army had taken an enemy capital in the Western Hemisphere in the century.

The war ended with the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, signed February 2, 1848. Mexico recognized the Rio Grande as the Texas border and ceded a vast territory, the Mexican Cession, covering present day California, Nevada, Utah, most of Arizona and New Mexico, and parts of Colorado and Wyoming, in exchange for fifteen million dollars and the assumption of some prior claims. In one stroke the United States had made real the continental vision behind Manifest Destiny and completed the territorial ambitions that Texas independence had begun.

Victory brought a bitter aftertaste. As soon as fighting began, Pennsylvania congressman David Wilmot proposed banning slavery in any territory won from Mexico, and though his Wilmot Proviso never became law, it exposed how the new land reopened the very sectional argument over slavery that Americans had tried to bury under compromise for decades. Critics like Henry David Thoreau, who spent a night in jail in 1846 for refusing to pay a tax he associated with the war, saw the conflict as a land grab for slaveholders rather than a mission of liberty, a debate that would only grow louder in the years ahead.
